newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan Takefuji's profits up on cash-machine loans.
newsitem.headline: Japan Takefuji's profits up on cash-machine loans.

text.p: More and more Japanese are heading for cash dispensers to borrow cash, boosting earnings at the operators of such systems, but industry leader Takefuji Corp is still struggling to improve its image.
The company said on Thursday that its parent current profit for the six months to September hit a record 60.06 billion yen ($536 million), surging 23 percent from a year ago.
Current profit is pre-tax and includes losses and gains on non-operating activities such as investments in shares.

"The healthy half-year earnings of Takefuji are probably a surprise even to the company's officials," Koya Hasegawa, analyst at Nikko Research Institute, said. "But the corporate image is somewhat tainted and investors may still be reluctant to invest in the company despite the solid earnings."

Personal loan companies were formerly criticised as loan sharks living off of the financially troubled. But in recent years, some have polished up their businesses and gone public. Takefuji listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange in August.

Tabloids have tried to uncover blemishes in Takefuji's past ever since the company's debut on the market. In October, the market was jarred by news that a former finance ministry official was offered shares in the firm before it went public.
Neither party broke any laws in the deal, but ministry officials have been asked to refrain from share transactions after recent scandals over bureaucrats' close ties with the business world.

Despite such news, the Japanese are finding that the automatic telling machines (ATMs), strategically placed near stations and shopping malls, are a great way of getting cash although they have to finance these borrowings by credit.

Takefuji said it installed 113 new ATMs across Japan in the half year, bringing the total to 767. As a result, its outstanding loans ballooned by more than 16 percent from the same period a year ago to 1.00 trillion yen ($8.9 billion).
Other consumer finance companies such as Acom Co Ltd and Promise Co Ltd also reaped record high profits due to an increase in borrowings through ATMs.

Analysts said that although the loans were increasing, consumer finance companies were relatively safe from damage from non-performing loans, as their loans are targetted at individuals and so are not staggering sums.

"The environment couldn't be better for the industry," Hasegawa said. "Customers are increasing, Japan's bank interest rates are at historical lows -- for an industry which relies on banks for funds, the procurement costs can't get any smaller."

But Takefuji's share price has been dwindling, unlike those of its rivals. Judging from company performance, Takefuji shares should be above the 10,000 yen ($89) level, and if the price does not improve soon while interest rates are low, it may never be able to, stock brokers said.
The shares were at 8,250 yen ($73) at the close of trade in Tokyo on Thursday, down 20 yen (18 cents).
"Takefuji can only hope the dust will settle and no new damaging media reports will emerge," one broker said.
